label: Modifier
item_text: A textual string may refer to a disease name, but it may modify a noun phrase (or may not be a noun phrase itself). In such cases, annotate using the **Modifier** category.
- **Specific Disease**: Mentions that can be linked to one specific definition that does not include further categorization.

label: Modifier
item_text: - When the disease is named in such a phrase (e.g., “ovarian cancer cases”), the named disease is a **Modifier** (§3).

label: Modifier
item_text: IF a disease-denoting span (a full disease name or its acronym) occupies the leftmost premodifier slot of a noun phrase whose head denotes a molecular entity (a gene, protein, or similar nomenclature-bearing noun, including forms with numeric or designator suffixes), THEN annotate the disease span as **Modifier**. The molecular status of the head does not license an O label for the disease span.

label: Modifier
item_text: - (a) the deficit term is adjectival or predicative (e.g., “G6PD deficient,” “[enzyme] deficient”). Annotate these as **Modifier**.
Use the smallest span necessary to include all tokens expressing the most specific form of the disease.

label: Composite Mention
item_text: A textual string may refer to two or more separate disease mentions. Such mentions are annotated with the **Composite Mention** category.
Abbreviation definitions such as “Huntington disease” (“HD”) are separated into two annotated mentions (one for the long form, one for the abbreviation).
- **Disease Class**: Mentions that could be described as a family of multiple specific diseases.

label: Specific Disease
item_text: IF a noun phrase’s head is a nominal deficit or loss-of-function term (such as “deficiency,” “absence,” or “deficient activity” used as a noun) and takes an “of” or “in” complement that names a gene, enzyme, or protein as the defective entity, AND the phrase denotes a congenital or inherited deficiency state, THEN annotate the entire noun phrase, including the complement, as **Specific Disease**. A premodifying biomolecule name before a final deficit head (e.g., “C7 deficiency,” “glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency”) falls under the same rule.

label: Specific Disease
item_text: If a disease mention is a bare, unmodified head noun with no proper name, eponym, or acronym (singular or plural), and the noun is predicated of a particular individual, case, or genotype, annotate it as **Specific Disease**, regardless of whether its lexical meaning suggests a superordinate category. Anchoring cues include:
- However, the terms “cancer” and “tumor” were retained (but see #8 for bare cohort descriptors).
- a presenting or diagnostic predicate (e.g., “presenting with/as X,” “was found to have X”), or

- it is the complement of a disease-characterizing predicate whose subject is the disease mention (or its disease-category head), such as “X is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by …”, or it is an item in a coordinated list that follows such a predicate;

label: Disease Class
item_text: - the noun is a superordinate category grouping multiple named conditions (e.g., “types of X,” “a class of X disorders”). It remains **Disease Class**.
For each sentence in the PubMed abstract and title, the locations of all disease mentions are marked, including duplicates within the same sentence.
